verdicts.text: In both Pulumi ESC and Vault, secrets can be stored and accessed through a CLI, SDK, or editor interface.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) HashiCorp's docs say Vault "exposes all features through the HTTP API, and both the CLI and UI internally rely on these same API calls." HashiCorp also maintains official client libraries (SDKs) for reading and writing secrets from application code. For ESC, it's well established that you can use the ESC CLI, SDKs, and the Pulumi Cloud environment editor, but this search didn't independently confirm that part.
verdicts.framing_note: "Editor interface" for Vault matches its web UI, which is looser wording than the source uses. The ESC half is a claim about Pulumi's own product and wasn't checked against product source.

verdicts.text: In both Pulumi ESC and Vault, secrets can be stored and accessed through a CLI, SDK, or editor interface.
verdicts.evidence: The ESC side checks out: the public pulumi/esc-sdk repo exists, and ESC ships a CLI (`pulumi env`) and a Pulumi Cloud editor. For Vault, I'm going on well-known product facts (the `vault` CLI, official client libraries and a web UI editor), not on a Vault page I fetched this session.
verdicts.source: gh search repos esc-sdk --owner pulumi (pulumi/esc-sdk public); repo:content/docs/esc/vs/vault.md L69-81 (context only)
verdicts.framing_note: The Vault half was not confirmed from a Vault source in this session. A pass3 check against HashiCorp docs would raise confidence.

verdicts.text: HashiCorp Vault is not open source and uses the Business Source License model.
verdicts.evidence: HashiCorp's own announcement (Aug 2023) says it is changing "from Mozilla Public License v2.0 (MPL 2.0) to the Business Source License (BSL, also known as BUSL) v1.1 on all future releases of HashiCorp products." The same post calls BSL 1.1 "a source-available license" and not an open-source one. Independent coverage adds that BSL "does not meet the traditional definition of open source as described by the Open Source Initiative."
verdicts.framing_note: Only Vault releases since August 2023 use BSL. Older Vault versions stay under MPL 2.0, which is open source, but the claim is accurate for current Vault.

verdicts.text: Pulumi ESC is fully open source and Apache 2.0 licensed.
verdicts.evidence: The pulumi/esc repo (the evaluation engine and CLI) is licensed "Apache-2.0" according to the GitHub API, so the license part is accurate. But the same page describes ESC's hosting as a "Fully managed SaaS service provided by Pulumi Cloud", and that service backend isn't open source. So "fully open source" says more than the Apache-licensed repo supports.
verdicts.source: gh api repos/pulumi/esc (license: Apache-2.0); repo:content/docs/esc/vs/vault.md L52
verdicts.framing_note: overclaim: the source says the 'pulumi/esc repo is Apache-2.0', but the claim says 'ESC is fully open source'. ESC's Pulumi Cloud service is proprietary.
verdicts.intuition_flag: The word "fully" is the problem. ESC runs as a Pulumi Cloud SaaS, and only the engine and CLI are open source.

verdicts.text: Pulumi ESC provides composability of collections of secrets and configuration, such that environments can be composed together from multiple other environments, so shared configuration is inherited rather than duplicated.
verdicts.evidence: The ESC imports concept page says: "Pulumi ESC allows you to compose environments by importing configuration and secrets from other environments. This reduces duplication... from any number of other environments." Explicit imports merge the imported values into the importing environment with JSON Merge Patch, which backs the "inherited rather than duplicated" wording.
verdicts.framing_note: Confidence is medium because the only support is a Pulumi docs page (corroboration only). I couldn't check the pulumi/esc source because the gh search hit its rate limit.

verdicts.text: Pulumi ESC environments can be composed together from multiple other environments, so shared configuration is inherited rather than duplicated.
verdicts.evidence: The pulumi/esc README (under "How Pulumi ESC Works") says: "Pulumi ESC enables you to define environments, which are collections of secrets and configuration. Each environment can be composed from multiple environments." Composing environments this way (via imports) is what lets shared configuration be inherited instead of copied.

verdicts.text: Pulumi ESC and Vault can be used together to store and manage infrastructure and application secrets.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) The ESC vault-secrets provider docs page (not the page under review) says: "The `vault-secrets` provider enables you to dynamically import secrets from HashiCorp Vault into your environment." A companion vault-login provider handles OIDC or token authentication to Vault, so the two products can be used together.
verdicts.framing_note: The live copy of vault.md says the same thing but is the reviewed file, so it isn't used as evidence. The integration is confirmed by the separate provider reference pages, which are synced from the ESC API schema.

verdicts.text: Through Pulumi ESC, secrets stored in Vault can be organized as collections that are versioned, branched, and composed inside other collections.
verdicts.evidence: The ESC CLI source (pulumi/esc cmd/esc/cli) has environment clone (env_clone.go), diff and versioning commands, and ESC environments can import one another. That covers "versioned" and "composed inside other collections". "Branched" fits only loosely: ESC has no native branch concept, and the closest match is cloning (forking) an environment, which the page's own table calls "forked for testing".
verdicts.source: gh api repos/pulumi/esc/contents/cmd/esc/cli (env_clone.go, env_diff.go, env_edit.go, env_open.go)
verdicts.intuition_flag: "Branched" is marketing language for environment cloning/forking; ESC has no real branch feature.

verdicts.text: HashiCorp Vault offers a hosted cloud service and self-hosting, and self-hosting requires significant management overhead.
verdicts.evidence: HashiCorp docs confirm both options: HCP Vault Dedicated is "a fully managed implementation of Vault Enterprise," while Vault Enterprise and Community Edition are self-managed. HashiCorp pitches HCP as a way to "reduce operational overhead" through managed upgrades and backups, which implies self-hosting carries that overhead. How "significant" the overhead is remains a subjective judgment.
verdicts.intuition_flag: The lighter SaaS option, HCP Vault Secrets, reached end of sale in June 2025, and remaining customers had to migrate off it by July 1, 2026. The only hosted Vault offering left is HCP Vault Dedicated, so check that the page doesn't mention Vault Secrets.

verdicts.text: HashiCorp Vault provides a key-value store.
verdicts.evidence: The Pulumi Vault provider, which is bridged from Vault's API, ships a `kv` module with `Secret`, `SecretV2`, `SecretBackendV2`, `getSecretV2` and `getSecretsListV2`. These map to Vault's KV (key-value) secrets engine versions 1 and 2, which confirms Vault provides a key-value store.
verdicts.framing_note: This is indirect evidence: I got it from the provider's SDK surface, not from HashiCorp's own docs. The code search was rate-limited.

verdicts.text: HashiCorp Vault offers a key/value form editor with a JSON toggle for editing and authoring, which is limited compared to Pulumi ESC.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) HashiCorp's official tutorial confirms the Vault UI KV form comes with a JSON toggle: "Instead of entering the key-value pairs one by one, you can enter the secret values using JSON." The "limited compared to Pulumi ESC" part is a comparative opinion, not something a source can confirm or refute.
verdicts.framing_note: Factual part (KV form editor plus JSON toggle) is confirmed. "Limited" is the author's own subjective comparison.

verdicts.text: Pulumi ESC is available as `pulumi env` in the Pulumi CLI and supports injecting application secrets as environment variables and modifying secrets.
verdicts.evidence: The auto-generated CLI reference lists `pulumi env` ("Manage environments"). Its subcommands include `pulumi env run` ("Open the environment with the given name and run a command."), which covers injecting secrets as environment variables. They also include `pulumi env set` ("Set a value within an environment."), `edit`, and `remove`, which cover modifying secrets.

verdicts.text: The `vault` CLI reads and writes secrets but does not inject them as environment variables; Vault Agent's process supervisor mode covers that separately.
verdicts.evidence: HashiCorp docs confirm that Vault Agent's Process Supervisor Mode "allows Vault secrets to be injected into a process via environment variables using Consul Template markup", using env_template and exec blocks. None of the results mention env injection in the regular vault CLI read/write commands, but that negative part is inferred from docs being silent, not stated outright.
verdicts.framing_note: The source confirms the Agent process-supervisor half. The claim that "the CLI does not inject" rests on the docs not mentioning it. Note that Vault Agent itself is started through the same binary (`vault agent`), so "separately" means a separate mode, not a separate tool.

verdicts.text: HashiCorp Vault supports a declarative provider such that individual secrets can be managed as resources with the Vault provider for Pulumi or Terraform.
verdicts.evidence: The Pulumi Vault provider has a vault.kv.SecretV2 resource, and its registry reference says it "Writes a KV-V2 secret to a given path in Vault." The same page shows the matching Terraform resource `vault_kv_secret_v2`, so individual secrets can be managed as resources in both Pulumi and Terraform.
verdicts.framing_note: The provider schema defines per-secret resources (kv.SecretV2, kv.Secret) that map to Terraform's vault_kv_secret_v2. That proves the claim's statement that individual secrets can be managed declaratively.

verdicts.text: Pulumi ESC supports a declarative provider via the Pulumi Service Provider, which allows management (create, update, delete) of collections of secrets and configuration as a resource through infrastructure as code.
verdicts.evidence: The Pulumi Service Provider (pulumi/pulumi-pulumiservice) has a `PulumiServiceEnvironmentResource` in provider/pkg/resources/environment.go. It takes org, project, name and yaml inputs and implements Create (`CreateEnvironmentWithProject` then `UpdateEnvironmentWithRevision` with the yaml), Delete (`DeleteEnvironment`) and Diff, so ESC environments can be managed as IaC resources.
verdicts.framing_note: The output was cut off before the Update method, but update is shown by `UpdateEnvironmentWithRevision` and the non-replace yaml diff. The claim's "collections of secrets and configuration" means ESC environments.

verdicts.text: HashiCorp Vault individual secrets can be managed as resources with the Vault provider for Pulumi or Terraform.
verdicts.evidence: The Pulumi Vault provider (pulumi/pulumi-vault) ships a `vault.kv.Secret` resource (sdk/nodejs/kv/secret.ts), so individual Vault secrets can be managed as resources. The Pulumi provider is bridged from the Terraform Vault provider, which has the same resource (vault_kv_secret).

verdicts.text: Pulumi ESC supports composability such that hierarchical environments inherit values from the environments they import.
verdicts.evidence: The ESC imports concept page says: "Pulumi ESC allows you to compose environments by importing configuration and secrets from other environments... enables you to organize configuration hierarchically", and "values from the imported environments are merged into the current environment using a JSON Merge Patch." One exception: an import marked `merge: false` does not merge its values automatically.
verdicts.framing_note: This is corroborated by a Pulumi docs page, not product source. GitHub code search hit a rate limit (HTTP 429), so I couldn't check it against pulumi/esc.

verdicts.text: HashiCorp Vault secrets versioning is limited in that secrets are individually versioned.
verdicts.evidence: Vault's KV v2 API docs describe versioning as per key: "max_versions (int: 0) – The number of versions to keep per key." The factual part, that secrets are versioned one at a time, holds up (and KV v1 has no versioning at all). Calling this "limited" is Pulumi's own comparison with ESC's environment-level versioning, not something Vault's docs say.
verdicts.framing_note: No source is cited in the claim. "Limited" is editorial comparison. The checkable part (versioning per key/secret) matches HashiCorp docs.

verdicts.text: In Pulumi ESC, environments can import secrets from another environment, and secrets updated from the referenced environment automatically propagate to downstream environments.
verdicts.evidence: The ESC imports concept page says environments can import "configuration and secrets from other environments" and that "The `imports` key is a list of environments that are resolved at runtime." Since imports are resolved at runtime, updates to the imported environment reach downstream environments. One caveat: imports pinned to a version tag or revision (vault.md L95) would not pick up later changes.
verdicts.framing_note: "Automatically propagate" is inferred from "resolved at runtime"; no page states it word for word. This supporting evidence is another docs page (same-site), not product source.

verdicts.text: HashiCorp Vault does not support interpolating values from other values.
verdicts.evidence: Vault's KV engine docs don't describe any way for a stored value to reference or interpolate another value. On HashiCorp Discuss, users ask how to do this, e.g. "wondering if it supports referencing another key within the same secret", and the snippets I found show no native feature. This is circumstantial: there's no official statement that the feature doesn't exist.
verdicts.intuition_flag: This is a bare absolute claim. Vault Agent / consul-template templating can combine several secret values on the client side, so the word "interpolating" could be challenged. Server-side KV interpolation does appear to be missing.

verdicts.text: HashiCorp Vault does not support branching or personal configs.
verdicts.evidence: Vault's KV v2 docs only describe linear versioning ("a key can retain a configurable number of versions"). No branching feature is documented, but no official page says outright that branching is unsupported. "Personal configs" is too vague to check: Vault has per-token cubbyhole storage and per-user paths through templated ACL policies, which could count as personal secret spaces.
verdicts.source: https://developer.hashicorp.com/vault/docs/secrets/kv; WebSearch ran query "HashiCorp Vault KV secrets engine versioning branching"
verdicts.intuition_flag: This is a competitor-absence claim. The "no branching" part is plausible, but "no personal configs" may overstate it given Vault's cubbyhole and identity-templated per-user paths.

verdicts.text: The `pulumi env diff` command shows the changes between two environments or two versions of a single environment.
verdicts.evidence: The ESC CLI source defines the env diff command's long help text as "This command displays the changes between two environments or two versions of a single environment." `pulumi env` is built from this same ESC CLI command set.
verdicts.framing_note: The claim restates the command's own Long help text almost word for word.

verdicts.text: HashiCorp Vault does not support comparing secrets across environments.
verdicts.evidence: Third-party comparisons, all written by competing vendors, say Vault has no built-in way to compare environments. Doppler says Vault "does not provide a visual diffing mechanism for comparing application secrets between environments." Infisical says Vault has "no native concept of environments," so users simulate environments with path structures and compare values by hand.
verdicts.framing_note: The sources say Vault lacks a native or visual diff feature. The claim's "does not support comparing" is a bit stronger, because you can still compare paths manually.
verdicts.intuition_flag: The evidence for this absence claim comes only from competitor marketing, and I found no official HashiCorp statement. Consider rewording to "no built-in/native comparison".

verdicts.text: Pulumi ESC supports built-in functions including `toJSON`, `fromJSON`, `fromBase64`, and `toString` that allow data manipulation for any scenario.
verdicts.evidence: In pulumi/esc, merged PR #117 is titled "eval: add fn::from{Base64,JSON}", and PR #628 "Fix fn::toString quoting" shows that fn::toString exists. fn::toJSON is a standard ESC built-in, but I didn't confirm it directly in source because code search hit a rate limit. "For any scenario" is marketing language, not something you can check.
verdicts.source: gh pr list -R pulumi/esc --state all --search "fromBase64 OR toJSON OR fromJSON OR toString"
verdicts.intuition_flag: "Allows data manipulation for any scenario" is an unfalsifiable overstatement. Consider softening it.

verdicts.text: HashiCorp Vault provides templating and transformation functions, such as username templating and the Transform secrets engine, rather than functions for composing configuration values.
verdicts.evidence: Vault's docs confirm both examples: "Username templating are used in some secret engines to allow operators to define how dynamic usernames are generated," using Go templates plus extra functions, and the Transform secrets engine has its own documentation. The part saying Vault has no functions for composing configuration values is a comparison. The core server has no config-composition function language, but that part is only partly supported: Vault Agent templating and VSO secret transformation use Go templates to render secrets into config files.
verdicts.framing_note: Both named features are confirmed by Vault docs. The claim that Vault lacks composition functions is the author's characterization, not a statement from a source.
verdicts.intuition_flag: "Rather than functions for composing configuration values" may undersell Vault Agent/Consul Template and VSO templating, which do compose secrets into config output. The Transform engine is also Enterprise-only (ADP), and the claim doesn't say so.

verdicts.text: Both Pulumi ESC and HashiCorp Vault provide audit logs.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) HashiCorp's Vault docs say "Audit logs record the details of every request received and response sent by the Vault API" through audit devices. Audit devices are off by default and have to be turned on. For ESC, the pulumi/esc README says "All actions taken on environments, secrets, or configuration values are fully logged for auditing," and the Pulumi Cloud audit log event reference lists events for opening, reading and editing ESC environments.
verdicts.framing_note: The claim names no source. It says both products offer audit logs, and each vendor's own docs confirm that. Two caveats: Vault audit devices are disabled by default, and Pulumi Cloud audit logs may be limited to some pricing tiers. Neither makes the claim false.

verdicts.text: HashiCorp Vault uses a security barrier for all requests made to the backend, and the security barrier automatically encrypts all data leaving Vault using a 256-bit Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) cipher in Galois Counter Mode (GCM) with 96-bit nonces.
verdicts.evidence: HashiCorp's Security Model page says "Vault uses a security barrier for all requests made to the backend," and that the barrier "automatically encrypts all data leaving Vault using a 256-bit Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) cipher in the Galois Counter Mode (GCM) with 96-bit nonces." The Vault source (barrier_aes_gcm.go) backs this up: it uses a 12-byte nonce and a 256-bit key.
verdicts.framing_note: The claim repeats the HashiCorp docs sentences almost word for word.

verdicts.text: Pulumi ESC uses TLS for encryption in transit and employs unique encryption keys per environment for encryption at rest.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) Public ESC docs confirm that secrets are encrypted at rest ("Any value wrapped in fn::secret is encrypted at rest and masked in output"). No fetched source confirmed TLS in transit or unique encryption keys per environment. The only per-scope key statement found covers IaC stacks, not ESC environments ("a key managed by the app.pulumi.com service, specific to your stack").
verdicts.source: https://www.pulumi.com/docs/esc/operations/managing-secrets/; https://www.pulumi.com/blog/managing-secrets-with-pulumi/; WebSearch ran query "Pulumi ESC encryption at rest unique key per environment TLS"
verdicts.intuition_flag: The "unique encryption keys per environment" detail may come from the Pulumi Cloud stack key model, not documented ESC behavior; check it against the ESC FAQ or product source.

verdicts.text: Both Pulumi ESC and HashiCorp Vault provide access controls.
verdicts.evidence: The pricing page describes Pulumi Cloud access controls ("including RBAC for advanced policy controls"), and ESC runs in Pulumi Cloud, which has environment-level permissions. Vault's ACL policy system is well known, and the page's own line 19 notes that Vault has "comprehensive access policies." I couldn't read an ESC-specific access-control doc because GitHub search hit its rate limit.
verdicts.framing_note: Broad yes/no capability claim from a comparison-table row. Both products clearly have access controls.

verdicts.text: HashiCorp Vault's cloud secrets engines generate short-lived credentials for AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud, with each engine configured with a static credential that Vault uses to mint them.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) The first part is right: Vault's AWS, Azure, and GCP secrets engines do generate dynamic, short-lived credentials. The second part is too absolute. Vault's AWS API docs say "Credentials can be configured either with IAM access keys for a privileged AWS account, or using Plugin Workload Identity Federation (WIF)." HashiCorp also says plugin WIF "is available for AWS, GCP, and Azure secret engines," which means those engines don't need a stored static credential.
verdicts.framing_note: overclaim — the docs present static keys and WIF as two options ("either with IAM access keys ... or using Plugin Workload Identity Federation"); the claim says every engine is configured with a static credential.
verdicts.intuition_flag: WIF is an Enterprise feature, so the claim is roughly true for Vault Community Edition. It is still wrong as a blanket statement, and the AWS engine can also get credentials from an instance profile or the environment through the AWS SDK.

verdicts.text: Pulumi Cloud can be used as an OIDC provider from the Pulumi SDK, CLI, UI, and the `pulumi-service` provider.
verdicts.evidence: The provider ships an `OidcIssuer` resource ("Register an OIDC Provider to establish a trust relationship between third-party systems like GitHub Actions and Pulumi Cloud"). Its examples register Pulumi Cloud's own issuer with `url: "https://api.pulumi.com/oidc"`, so Pulumi Cloud does act as an OIDC provider and the provider can manage OIDC. I didn't check the SDK, CLI and UI parts of the claim one by one.
verdicts.source: gh search code --repo pulumi/pulumi-pulumiservice oidc (provider/pkg/resources/oidc_issuer.go, examples/api/oidc-issuer/*)
verdicts.framing_note: The provider source confirms OIDC issuer management. The claim also lists SDK, CLI and UI access, which is plausible but wasn't confirmed one by one.
verdicts.intuition_flag: The provider's actual name is `pulumiservice` (repo pulumi/pulumi-pulumiservice), not `pulumi-service`. The row also mixes two ideas: Pulumi Cloud issuing OIDC tokens, and Pulumi Cloud trusting outside OIDC issuers.

verdicts.text: Configuring HashiCorp Vault as an OIDC provider is only available from the CLI.
verdicts.evidence: HashiCorp's OIDC identity provider docs show CLI (`vault write identity/oidc/...`) and HTTP API (curl) examples. None of the pages I fetched says configuration is "only available from the CLI," and none showed a UI or other way to configure it either. HashiCorp's Vault 1.10 blog only says OIDC provider support "is now generally available."
verdicts.source: https://developer.hashicorp.com/vault/docs/secrets/identity/oidc-provider; https://www.hashicorp.com/en/blog/vault-1-10; WebSearch ran query "Vault changelog "OIDC Provider" UI ..."
verdicts.intuition_flag: "Only from the CLI" is doubtful. Anything the Vault CLI does goes through the HTTP API, which also means Terraform, and newer Vault versions are believed to have an OIDC Provider section in the web UI (Access > OIDC Provider), though I couldn't confirm that in this session. The claim is probably stale.
